claims.text: Premelting onset in HEA nanoparticles is primarily governed by enhanced surface atomic diffusion.
High surface energy and surface defects promote surface atomic diffusion in HEA nanoparticles.
Rapid nanoscale synthesis produces a high density of surface defects or irregularities in HEA nanoparticles.
HEA nanoparticles smaller than 100 nm can contain multiple elements uniformly distributed within individual particles.
High configurational entropy in the multielement core stabilizes its crystalline structure.
A disordered, liquid-like surface layer develops well below the complete or bulk melting temperature.
Premelting produces a radial gradient from a disordered surface to an ordered core.
Nanoscale curvature lowers the energy barrier for surface atomic mobility.
Synthesis-induced surface defects lower the energy barrier for surface atomic mobility and induce a premelt layer.
Configurational-entropy stabilization of the HEA core delays complete melting.
Competition between surface-induced disordering and entropy-driven core stabilization governs overall premelting and melting.
HEA nanoparticles will form an earlier or more pronounced premelt surface layer than size- and morphology-matched mono- or binary nanoparticles.
Mono- or binary nanoparticles will melt more uniformly or exhibit premelting only closer to their bulk melting point.
The surface-to-core disorder gradient will be more pronounced in HEA nanoparticles than in mono- or binary controls.
The proposed mechanism should apply to nanoparticles below approximately 100 nm but may not apply to bulk materials or substantially larger particles.
The relevant premelting regime is typically below 0.5-0.6 times the constituent-metal melting temperature.
Nanoparticle-support interactions may additionally influence the thermal behavior.
